tldr: We introduce RAPID, a framework that automatically boots up a simulation environment, task specifications, and optimization-based action primitives from a single human demonstration video, acquiring robot programs that generalize across diverse environments through an agentic coding loop.
hero_caption: Overview of RAPID. From just a single human demonstration video (flipping upright and lifting a cereal box), it automatically generates an object-centric relational program. The robot successfully completes the task in novel scenes with significantly different object shapes, placements, and textures.
overview:
As LLM-powered coding agents achieve strong results in software engineering, generating robot manipulation code automatically has attracted growing attention. However, running an agentic loop where the agent writes, runs, verifies, and fixes code requires three key ingredients: task success conditions, executable action primitives, and an interactive simulation environment for trial-and-error verification. Prior methods assumed humans manually prepared all three, falling short of true autonomy.

To tackle this, the authors developed RAPID, a framework that automatically constructs all three elements starting from just a single human demonstration video. It reconstructs 3D objects from the initial video frame to spin up a MuJoCo environment, and infers success predicates and trajectory-optimization primitives from each phase of the video. Furthermore, by expressing the strategy through geometric relationships between objects rather than absolute coordinates, RAPID achieves high reusability that remains robust against variations in placement and object geometry.

The authors evaluated RAPID on eight challenging contact-rich nonprehensile manipulation tasks requiring pushing, toppling, or pivoting, on the LIBERO-Pro benchmark, and on a physical Franka arm. Without any pre-defined primitives or human-engineered reward functions, RAPID demonstrated strong generalization across novel scenes with varying object poses, shapes, and physical parameters like friction.
contributions: Proposed RAPID, a framework that automatically infers task specifications, action primitives, and an interactive verification environment from a single visual human demonstration to close the autonomous coding loop.

Introduced the Object-Centric Relational Program representation (OReP), which avoids absolute object coordinates and instead solves run-time trajectory optimization based on geometric relations and desired effects, enabling high reusability and generalization.

Demonstrated superior success rates over prior baselines without pre-defined primitives across eight contact-rich nonprehensile tasks, the prehensile-focused LIBERO-Pro benchmark, and a real-world Franka arm.

sections.heading: Why run an agentic coding loop from demonstration videos?
sections.summary: The true strength of coding agents lies in the iterative loop of generation, execution, verification, and refinement. In robotics, setting up verification environments and primitives has been a major roadblock. This work introduces RAPID, which autonomously builds all of them from a single human demo video to synthesize and generalize contact-rich manipulation programs.
sections.details:
Recent advances in coding agents have been remarkable. When human engineers program robot behaviors, they follow an iterative process: write code, run it, observe failures, and fix it. We want autonomous agents to run this same agentic coding loop. However, realizing this in robotics faces three key barriers:

- A testable task specification (criteria for judging success)
- Action primitives bridging to low-level control (unit motions such as pushing, toppling, or grasping)
- An interactive environment (simulator) where the agent can reset and perform trial-and-error indefinitely

Existing work assumes humans provide these components beforehand. But that defeats the purpose of autonomy if a human must recreate environments and functions for every new task.

RAPID addresses this by leveraging a single human demonstration video. A video visually captures both the steps and the goal required to accomplish the task. RAPID reconstructs a 3D simulation environment from the video, infers success criteria for each motion, generates primitive code, and automatically tests and debugs the program in simulation. Instead of hard-coding coordinate values, it represents the program via geometric relations between objects, acquiring strategies that directly generalize to unseen scenes and novel objects.

captions.F2: Overview of the RAPID workflow. A verification environment is reconstructed from the demo video via Real2Sim. The coding agent then receives feedback to iteratively refine a strategy program composed of optimization-based primitives and relational constraints.

sections.heading: How RAPID stands apart from prior research
sections.summary: We organize related work into three areas: program generation for robotics, learning from few demonstrations, and nonprehensile manipulation. RAPID sets itself apart by autonomously synthesizing and refining everything from a demonstration, without relying on fixed primitives or pre-defined environments.
sections.details:
This work sits at the intersection of three main research areas.

### Programming for Robotics
Approaches like Code as Policies (CaP) prompt LLMs to write code, CaP-X incorporates feedback loops, and Voyager expands skill libraries over time. However, these methods assume reward functions, human-crafted primitive functions, and resettable environments are provided beforehand. RAPID fundamentally differs by generating all three directly from a demonstration video.

### Learning from Few Demonstrations
Methods for generalizing from few demonstrations have explored geometric correspondence estimation, contact structure transfer, and subgoal decomposition. Yet these techniques remain confined to rigid learning pipelines or fixed planner frameworks. RAPID combines an object-centric relational program representation with iterative agentic code refinement to construct flexible, reusable strategies.

### Nonprehensile Manipulation
Nonprehensile motions such as pushing, pivoting, toppling, and sliding feature complex contact mechanics and resist simple standardized primitives like pick-and-place. Prior work relied on analytical mechanics models, complex trajectory optimization, or massive reinforcement learning. RAPID takes a fresh approach: the agent writes, verifies, and tunes the necessary contact primitives directly as code.

sections.heading: The full end-to-end mechanism of RAPID
sections.summary: RAPID takes only a demo video and a natural language instruction as input. It synthesizes primitives, connects them via relational constraints, and iteratively verifies them in simulation. Deploying to novel environments requires only resolving semantic object bindings in seconds.
sections.details:
The problem setting of RAPID is straightforward. The inputs are solely a single visual demonstration video $D$ capturing quasi-static rigid-body manipulation and a language instruction $l$. No task success signals, pre-existing action primitives, or initialized simulators are provided.

The entire process proceeds in three main steps:

- **1. Bootstrapping Environment and Specifications**: From the initial video frame, RAPID reconstructs a digital twin simulation environment. It then segments the video into phases and infers subgoals and success predicates for each phase.
- **2. Constructing and Verifying Primitives and Strategies**: The agent writes a local trajectory-optimization program (primitive) for each phase. It tests the primitive in simulation and autonomously repairs the code upon failure. Next, it assembles a complete strategy program chained by relational constraints and verifies it across randomly generated scene variations.
- **3. Deployment to Novel Scenes**: To deploy in a new real-world scene, RAPID detects objects from camera observations and binds them to the semantic roles required by the strategy program, such as target object, obstacle, or fixture. This semantic binding takes only a few seconds, and the optimized strategy code executes on the robot immediately without rewriting.

sections.heading: Why it works: Object-centric relational program representation
sections.summary: Recording motions in absolute coordinates makes them brittle to environmental changes. RAPID defines actions as local trajectory-optimization programs that achieve specific object effects, chaining them through geometric relational constraints conditioned on previous outcomes.
sections.details:
The cornerstone of RAPID's generalization ability is its Object-Centric Relational Program representation (OReP).

### IV-A Action Primitives as Local Trajectory Optimization
Rather than a fixed joint trajectory or a black-box policy, each primitive $P_i$ is coded as a local trajectory-optimization program composed of the following:

- **Semantic Interface ($C_i$)**: Defines the involved object roles $\mathbf{r}_i$ (e.g., target object, support surface, fixture, manipulator) and effect parameters $\mathbf{q}_i$ (e.g., toppling angle, push distance).
- **Geometric Resolver ($\rho_i$)**: A runtime function that computes geometric features, such as contact surfaces and rotation axes, from current observations.
- **Cost Function ($J_i$) and Optimization**: Consists of a terminal cost $J_i^{\mathrm{f}}$ measuring final state discrepancy and a path cost $J_i^{\mathrm{p}}$ ensuring contact stability. The agent writes this cost function along with initialization heuristics as code. It then searches for the optimal robot trajectory in simulation using the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM), a derivative-free sampling-based optimizer.

### IV-B Composing Strategies with Relational Constraints
The overall task strategy $\Pi$ chains multiple primitives serially using relational constraints $c_k$. By inspecting the environment state $s_{k-1}$ after phase $k-1$ concludes, the constraint dynamically computes the target argument $g_k$ for the subsequent phase $k$ right before execution (e.g., how many centimeters to push toward the gap between an obstacle and a fixture). Even if execution drifts slightly in an earlier phase, the next phase autonomously adjusts its goal.

### IV-C Deployment to Novel Scenes
In an unseen environment, the agent performs lightweight semantic role binding. The strategy and primitive code remain frozen and reused directly. Scene variations in geometry or friction are absorbed on the fly by the CEM trajectory optimization inside each primitive.

captions.F3: Example of composing primitives via relational constraints. Based on the object's pose after the flip phase and its geometric relationship with the fixture and obstacle, program $c_k$ dynamically computes and passes the displacement needed for the subsequent press move.

sections.heading: How code is generated, verified, and refined from demo videos
sections.summary: Using SAM 3D and MuJoCo, RAPID bootstraps a verification simulator from the first frame of a demo video. The agent segments the demo, derives success predicates, writes code, and iteratively debugs the program until it passes physically valid scene variations.
sections.details:
Here is the concrete pipeline of how RAPID synthesizes programs from a single demo video $(D, l)$.

### V-A Reconstructing an Interactive Simulation Environment
Verifying code requires an interactive environment. RAPID takes the initial RGB-D frame of the video and uses a VLM to infer semantic object labels and physical attributes such as mass and friction. It then extracts segmentation masks with SAM, reconstructs complete 3D meshes using SAM 3D, and aligns poses with FoundationPose to build a physics scene in MuJoCo. Furthermore, an automated sampler generates scene variations by perturbing object poses, friction, and dimensions. The agent also writes filter functions to reject physically invalid scene configurations, ensuring a valid test suite.

### V-B Autonomous Primitive Synthesis
A sub-agent temporally segments the video, inferring local subgoals and success predicates $\Psi_i$ for each segment. If no matching primitive exists in the library, the coding agent implements the new primitive interface, geometric resolver, and optimization cost function from scratch. It executes the primitive in the reconstructed environment and across scene variations, iteratively debugging and refining the code until all predicates $\Psi_i$ pass.

### V-C Task Strategy Integration and Verification
Once individual primitives are ready, the agent links them together via relational constraints $c_k$ based on the global task goal $G_\Pi$ and final predicate $\Psi_\Pi$ to form the full strategy program $\Pi$. It conducts full-horizon simulation verification. If failures occur, the agent fixes the relational constraint code connecting the phases, yielding the final robust strategy program.

sections.heading: Simulation and real-world evaluation: How far does it generalize?
sections.summary: We evaluated RAPID across eight nonprehensile tasks, the LIBERO-Pro benchmark, and a real Franka arm. Without human-designed primitives or reward signals, RAPID achieved high generalization success rates on 50 unseen scenes with varied appearances, shapes, and layouts, substantially outperforming baselines.
sections.details:
### VI-A Experimental Setup
The primary evaluation covers eight contact-rich nonprehensile manipulation tasks (T1–T8) involving flat-lying objects that cannot be grasped initially. These require sophisticated contact control, such as pushing into a slot, flipping upright against a wall, pivoting to create a gap, or toppling to grasp an edge. For testing, the authors curated 50 novel scenes with varying object shapes, sizes, appearances, materials, initial poses, and distractor obstacles.

Baselines include open-loop CaP without interaction, CaP+OReP incorporating this representation, CaP-Agent0 provided with ground-truth rewards and state feedback, and an ablation without scene variation generation. The underlying LLM is GPT-5.6 Sol in high-reasoning mode.

### VI-B Simulation Results on Nonprehensile Tasks
The results were decisive. Standard CaP and feedback-free CaP+OReP rarely succeeded, as inferring contact-rich relations without an execution-verification loop is extremely difficult. Moreover, RAPID outperformed the strong CaP-Agent0 baseline by a large margin, even though CaP-Agent0 had access to ground-truth success feedback and test-time code refinement. While CaP-Agent0 relied on hardcoded spatial offsets that failed under layout changes, RAPID adapted to real-time spatial variations through its geometric resolvers and local trajectory optimization.
Removing scene variation sampling (RAPID w/o SV) resulted in lower success rates and higher variance, confirming that pre-debugging over diverse scene variations is crucial for robustness.

### VI-C Generalization on LIBERO-Pro Benchmark
RAPID was also evaluated on the prehensile-centric LIBERO-Pro benchmark. Compared against Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models such as OpenVLA and $\pi_0$, as well as prior methods like ASPIRE, RAPID achieved the highest performance in 5 out of 6 settings. Notably, while ASPIRE requires pre-defined pick-and-place primitives, RAPID discovered its primitives autonomously from scratch while attaining superior success rates.

### VI-D Real-World Deployment on Franka Arm
The strategies obtained in simulation were deployed directly onto a physical Franka Research 3 arm. Thanks to real-time compliant impedance control and accurate physical parameter estimation via SAM 3D and VLMs, the Sim-to-Real gap was minimal. The system executed robustly across novel real-world objects in all eight nonprehensile tasks.

captions.F4: Snapshots of the physical Franka arm executing the eight nonprehensile tasks. The autonomously synthesized programs accomplish diverse, contact-rich behaviors including slot insertion (T1), flipping against fixtures (T2–T5), pivoting (T6), and domino toppling (T7).
captions.F5: Real-world experimental setup (left) and the diverse collection of everyday items and packaging used in the experiments (right). The system generalizes across objects with varying textures, dimensions, and stiffness without code modifications.

sections.heading: Summary and future directions
sections.summary: RAPID successfully closes the loop for coding agents using a single demonstration video, generating robot programs with strong generalization capabilities. Future work aims to integrate reinforcement learning for multi-fingered dexterous hands and expand to deformable object simulators.
sections.details:
This paper presented RAPID, a framework that bootstraps task specifications, action primitives, and an interactive simulation environment from a single visual human demonstration, synthesizing reusable robot programs through an agentic coding loop.

By formulating actions as object-centric trajectory-optimization programs linked by geometric relational constraints, RAPID achieves generalization capabilities that procedural code generation struggles to deliver. While generating and verifying code for a new task takes tens of minutes of compute time, this process is run only once; deploying the policy in novel scenes requires only a few seconds of semantic binding.

For future directions, the authors plan to incorporate reinforcement learning (RL) as a primitive learning tool to support multi-fingered dexterous hands, interface with simulation engines handling deformable objects like cloth and food, and further scale the framework as coding LLMs and robot foundation models advance.

takeaways: Leveraging coding agents in robotics requires closing the loop: rather than relying on one-shot code generation, the system must autonomously generate, execute, verify, and refine code in simulation.

Representing actions as geometric relations between objects coupled with local trajectory optimization (CEM)—rather than absolute coordinate sequences—yields high reusability against variations in object shape and pose.
Combining Real2Sim (SAM 3D + FoundationPose) with physical property estimation (VLMs) shows we can now automatically bootstrap practical digital twins for debugging directly from a single video.
limitations: Initial program synthesis and simulation verification require tens of minutes of compute per task, making the current pipeline unsuitable for instant, on-the-fly task learning.
Discovering robust primitives from a single debug scene remains challenging for tightly constrained articulated objects, such as opening and closing drawers, under significant spatial variations.
The current implementation is restricted to rigid-body manipulation; extending it to deformable objects, fluids, or complex in-hand manipulation with multi-fingered hands remains future work.
